newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets roll with US prices.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets roll with US prices.

text.p: Australian financial and equity markets are likely to come under pressure this week after higher-than-expected United States inflation data spooked U.S. markets and vindicated Federal Reserve Board governor Alan Greenspan's recent decision to hike interest rates.

The Producer Price Index (PPI), released last Friday, prompted a bond-market selloff and a Wall Street slump when it showed a 0.4 percent gain in its core component, even though the overall index declined 0.1 percent. Surges in aircraft and tobacco prices propelled the jump in core PPI.

U.S. and international markets are expected to trade nervously ahead of the release of U.S. March consumer prices this Tuesday, an indicator whose importance will override any local data to be issued this week.

According to a Reuters poll of economists and analysts, first quarter prices were expected up 0.2 percent overall and up 0.3 percent for the less-volatile core components -- those excluding food and evergy. A figure on par with the consensus would affect the market little, but any further increase in the core CPI could hurt U.S. bonds, some experts said.

Locally, February housing finance data on Monday is expected to create a bit of a stir, as the Australian Bankers Association data points to a large fall. Housing finance has risen by five percent in the last two months, but February's fall could easily reverse that, economists said.

If it did, it would add to some of the emerging doubts over the robustness of the economy in the early part of 1997 although it would be important to look at the components of the housing data, economists said.
Refinancing is expected to fall heavily, while finance for new housing and construction is expected to remain fairly strong.

Partial price data on Monday and Tuesday, (manufacturing and trade components) is expected to confirm that next week's local March quarter inflation data will be on the low side, while Westpac consumer sentiment is out on Wednesday.
The Reserve Bank bulletin is out on Monday, but it is not expected to contain anything that will concern the markets.
Finally, there is a possibility the long awaited outcome of the union movement's "living wage" claim could be released by the Industrial Relations tribunal.
BONDS: Fri 10-yr bond 92.015 (unch), 3-yr 92.99 (-0.01)

Australian bonds, while having a bid tone into the end of last week that is expected to remain ahead of next week's inflation data, are faced with the conflicting forces of postive local fundamentals but a bearish U.S. Treasuries market.

"I think people are thinking domestically the fundamentals aren't too bad and market probably represents value, I should be buying, but they're a little bit reluctant with the increasing expectation of them tightening in May in the States," one trader said.
"They want to buy it, but they are holding back," he said.

In a sign that the local market faces a difficult week, the US Treasuries market slumped on Friday in response to first quarter inflation data which was much higher than expected. The key 30-year bond yield soared to 7.17 percent, with analysts saying 7.25 percent was a near-term possibility.

While there is a possibility that the "living wage" decision could be released, traders said that the local market had been waiting on it for so long that if it came somewhere between A$10 and A$14 a week it would have minimal market impact.
The underlying positive tone to bonds has seen them outperforming other dollar-bloc debt, with spreads narrowing sharply on last Thursday's employment data.

With Monday's housing finance data expected to be supportive, inflation expected to be favourable and employment seen remaining soft, those spreads have the potential to narrow further in comning weeks, especially at the short end where
December bill futures still have a 50 point tightening factored in.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR: Fri local close US$0.7859, NY US$0.7847
The Australian dollar should build on last week's robust recovery which saw it surge from six-week lows at US$0.7735 to end Friday at (US$0.7847).

Dealers attributed much of the strength to offshore appetite for Australian debt which was seen offering attractive real yields even though spreads with the U.S. had narrowed since the Federal Reserve hiked U.S. interest rates by 25 basis points.

Japanese investors, in particular, were keen to earn higher returns offshore but had already invested so much in U.S. bonds that they were looking for other avenues, including Australian bonds, to diversify risk.
The risk of another U.S. tightening still lay like cloud ahead, however, and even a domestic easing could not be ruled if data continued as dire as last week's March employment report.
For this reason, many analysts felt the dollar would be hard pressed to sustain levels above 79 cents, although they were more optimistic about a test of the psychological 100.00 yen barrier.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS: Fri, All Ords Index 2,380.50 -12.40
Australian equities are likely to start the week with a downward bias after Wall Street tumbled 148 points on Friday due to a surprising jump in wholesale prices which reignited U.S. inflation fears.
Nervous trade last week saw a generally firm local mood restrained and the Dow's dive will keep a tight leash on any upside, at least early in the week.
"We are likely to see more of the same thin choppy business we saw last week," said one trader.
However, traders do not expect local losses to match the magnitude of Wall Street's with the underlying tone still considered reasonably firm.
In fact, local stocks were seen underpinned by the view that they were still good value.
"I'm getting very excited about our market. I think we are on the start of something," said a senior dealer at Brisbane-based broker.
Corporate events are thin on the ground.
On Tuesday, diamond miner Ashton Mining holds its annual meeting in Melbourne while Capral Aluminium has its annual meeting in Sydney.
Wednesday sees a general meeting of leisure group Village Roadshow while on Thursday major property group Westfield Holdings holds an extraordinary meeting.
In terms of economic data, February housing data on Monday is the key local release with a large fall expected.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
